library(tmap)

## Introduction

tmap is designed to be extended. This article gives an overview of the existing extension packages, the ways in which tmap can be extended, and how to get started.

## Extension packages

The following packages extend tmap. Together with tmap and the color palette package **cols4all**, they are called the *tmapverse*.

| package | what it adds | extends |
|---|---|---|
| [**tmap.mapgl**](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap.mapgl/) | the modes `"maplibre"` and `"mapbox"`, 3D polygons, and components such as a geocoder | modes, layers, components |
| [**tmap.glyphs**](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap.glyphs/) | glyphs: donuts, pies, and flowers | layers, scales |
| [**tmap.cartogram**](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap.cartogram/) | contiguous, non-contiguous, and Dorling cartograms | layers |
| [**tmap.networks**](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap.networks/) | networks: **sfnetworks** and **spatstat** `linnet` objects, edges and nodes | spatial data classes, layers |
| [**tmap.sources**](https://github.com/r-tmap/tmap.sources) | remote and tiled data sources, such as PMTiles and Overture Maps | spatial data classes |

The articles in the menu *Extensions* show these packages in action. An extension package does not have to be attached: its layer functions can also be called directly, e.g. `tmap.glyphs::tm_donuts()`. The function `tmap_overview()` shows which layers and components are available in which mode, and from which package they come.

## Ways to extend tmap

A map is made in three steps: spatial data are read, drawn as layers, and shown by a graphics engine (the mode). Each step can be extended:

1. [**Map layers**](#map-layers): what is drawn. A new layer may come with new map variables and a spatial transformation, e.g. `tm_donuts()` (**tmap.glyphs**) and `tm_cartogram()` (**tmap.cartogram**).
2. [**Spatial data classes**](#spatial-data-classes): what can be drawn, e.g. `sfnetwork` objects (**tmap.networks**).
3. [**Modes**](#modes): where it is drawn, e.g. `"maplibre"` (**tmap.mapgl**).

Two other building blocks can also be extended:

4. [**Map components**](#map-components): elements outside the data layers, e.g. `tm_geocoder()` (**tmap.mapgl**).
5. [**Scales**](#scales): how data values are mapped to visual values, e.g. `tm_scale_composition()` (**tmap.glyphs**). This is rarely needed, and the most difficult one.

The functions that are needed for extensions are exported and documented as internal functions, e.g. `?tmapScale`.

## Map layers

### Example: a spike map layer

The easiest way to create a new layer is to derive it from an existing one. As an example, we create a layer for *spike maps*: maps with a spike on each feature, with a height that is proportional to a data variable.

A spike is a line, so the new layer is derived from `tm_lines()`. Only the geometries have to be changed: each feature is replaced by a spike. This is done by a *spatial transformation function*. It takes the geometries (`shpTM$shp`), the values of the map variables that are used in the transformation (here `height`), and the arguments `args`, and returns new geometries with their IDs:

```{r}
tmapTransSpikes = function(shpTM, height, ord__, plot.order, args, scale) {
  shp = shpTM$shp
  pts = sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_point_on_surface(shp))
  bb = sf::st_bbox(shp)
  h = height / max(height, na.rm = TRUE) * args$height * (bb[4] - bb[2])
  w = args$width * (bb[3] - bb[1]) / 2
  spikes = lapply(seq_len(nrow(pts)), function(i) {
    x = pts[i, 1]
    y = pts[i, 2]
    sf::st_linestring(rbind(c(x - w, y), c(x, y + h[i]), c(x + w, y)))
  })
  list(shp = sf::st_sfc(spikes, crs = sf::st_crs(shp)), tmapID = shpTM$tmapID, bbox = shpTM$bbox)
}
```

The layer function creates a `tm_lines()` layer and changes a few of its fields:

* `layer`: the name of the new layer, followed by the layer it is derived from;
* `trans.fun`: the transformation function;
* `trans.aes`: the map variables that are used by the transformation, created with `tmapScale()`. Here, the data values are passed on as they are (`tm_scale_asis()`);
* `trans.args`: other arguments for the transformation function;
* `trans.apply_to`: `"this"` means that the transformation is only applied to this layer. With `"this_following"`, it is also applied to the layers that follow in the same `tm_shape()` group (used by cartograms).

```{r}
tm_spikes = function(height, max.height = 0.2, width = 0.01, ...) {
  layer = tm_lines(...)
  layer[[1]] = within(layer[[1]], {
    layer = c("spikes", "lines")
    trans.fun = tmapTransSpikes
    trans.aes = list(height = tmapScale(aes = "area", value = height, scale = tm_scale_asis(),
      legend = tm_legend_hide(), chart = tm_chart_none(), free = NA))
    trans.args = list(height = max.height, width = width)
    trans.apply_to = "this"
  })
  layer
}
```

The other arguments, such as `col` and `lwd`, are passed on to `tm_lines()`, so they work as usual, including scales and legends:

```{r, fig.height = 6.5}
tm_shape(NLD_muni) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey95", col = "grey80") +
tm_shape(NLD_muni) +
  tm_spikes(height = "population", width = 0.006, lwd = 1.5,
    col = "income_high",
    col.scale = tm_scale_intervals(values = "brewer.reds", values.range = c(0.3, 1)),
    col.legend = tm_legend("High income (%)"))
```

Since there is no plotting method for `"spikes"`, the plotting method of `"lines"` is used. Therefore, the new layer works in all modes, including view mode and the modes of **tmap.mapgl**. A layer that needs its own drawing, such as the donuts of **tmap.glyphs**, has a plotting method per mode (see [plotting methods](#plotting-methods)).

In a package, the transformation function is exported, and the layer function gets the arguments of `tm_lines()` explicitly, with documentation, as in `tmap.cartogram::tm_cartogram()`.

### The layer element

A layer function returns a list (`tm_element_list()`) with one `tm_element()`. The most important fields are:

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `layer` | the layer name, optionally followed by the layers it is derived from, e.g. `c("donuts", "symbols")` |
| `mapping.aes` | the map variables: a named list of `tmapScale()` objects (value, scale, legend, chart, and free) |
| `gpar` | the graphical parameters for drawing, created with `tmapGpar()`: `"__fill"` refers to the map variable `fill` |
| `trans.fun`, `trans.aes`, `trans.args`, `trans.apply_to` | the spatial transformation, e.g. `tmapTransCentroid()` for symbols |
| `tpar` | the transformation parameters (`tmapTpar()`) |
| `mapping.args` | other arguments for the plotting methods |
| `plot.order`, `zindex`, `group`, `popup.*`, `hover`, `id` | as in the standard layers |

### Spatial transformations

A spatial transformation function changes the geometries before they are drawn. It is called with the geometries (`shpTM`), the values of the map variables of `trans.aes`, the plotting order, and `trans.args`, as in the spike map example. It returns a list with the new geometries (`shp`), their IDs (`tmapID`), and the bounding box (`bbox`). tmap applies the transformation per facet, and reprojects the result to the crs of the map.

### Plotting methods

The layer is drawn by the plotting method of each mode: `tmapGridDataPlot()` (plot mode), `tmapLeafletDataPlot()` (view mode), and `tmapMaplibreDataPlot()` and `tmapMapboxDataPlot()` (**tmap.mapgl**). These are S3 generics that dispatch on the class `tm_data_<layer>`, e.g. `tmapGridDataPlot.tm_data_donuts()`. A method can modify the data, and then pass it on to the method of the layer it is derived from with `NextMethod()`, as **tmap.networks** does. If a layer has no method for a mode, the method of the layer it is derived from is used. The methods for the modes of **tmap.mapgl** are registered with `@exportS3Method tmap.mapgl::tmapMaplibreDataPlot`, so that **tmap.mapgl** is only needed when it is installed.

### New map variables

A layer may need a map variable that tmap does not have, such as `height` for 3D polygons in **tmap.mapgl**. A new map variable needs:

* default values, submitted with `tmapSubmitOptions()` in the `.onLoad()` function of the package: the constant value (`value.const`), the values for missing data (`value.na`), the default palettes or ranges (`values.var`, `values.range`), and the default scales (`scales.var`);
* functions named `tmapValues<Type>_<variable>()`, which are called by name: `Check` (are the visual values valid?), `IsDiv` (are they diverging?), `Range`, `Scale` (apply the global `scale`), `Colorize` (apply color effects, such as sepia), `VV` and `CVV` (the visual values for numeric and categorical scales), and `Submit`.

The functions of an existing map variable can often be reused, e.g. `tmapValuesCheck_height = tmap::tmapValuesCheck_size`. Use `tmap_options("value.const")` to see the defaults of the existing map variables.

## Spatial data classes

tmap supports **sf**, **stars**, **terra**, and **sp** objects. Another spatial data class is supported via S3 methods:

* `tmapShape()`: converts the object into geometries (`sfc` or a **stars** dimensions object) and a data table;
* `tmapGetShapeMeta1()` and `tmapGetShapeMeta2()`: return metadata, such as the names and levels of the data variables;
* `tmapSubsetShp()`: selects the data variables that are needed;
* `tmapReproject()`: only needed when the geometries are not converted to **sf** or **stars**, as in **tmap.sources**.

**tmap.networks** (classes `sfnetwork` and `linnet`) and **tmap.sources** (data sources specified by a character string) are examples. A new data class often comes with a layer for it, e.g. `tm_network()`.

## Modes

A mode is a graphics engine, such as **grid** (plot mode) and **leaflet** (view mode). This is the most extensive type of extension; **tmap.mapgl** is the reference implementation.

A new mode is registered with `tmapSubmitOptions(options = list(modes = list(<mode> = list(name = "<Name>", ...))))` in the `.onLoad()` function of the package. The list contains the options of the mode, and `<Name>` is used in the names of its functions, e.g. `tmapMaplibreInit()`:

* initialization and output: `Init`, `Shape` (per facet), `Overlay`, `Run`, `Arrange` (for `tmap_arrange()`), and `Providers` (basemaps);
* data layers: the S3 generic `DataPlot`, and `AuxPrepare` and `AuxPlot` for basemaps, tiles, and grid lines;
* components: the S3 generics `CompPrepare`, `CompWidth`, `CompHeight`, and `CompPlot`, and `Comp` for the legends;
* facet labels, axis labels, and grid labels: `Wrap`, `Xtab`, `Xlab`, `Ylab`, `GridXLab`, and `GridYLab`;
* **shiny** integration: methods for `tmapOutputGS()` and `tmapProxyGS()`.

Two other things make a new mode fit in with the existing ones:

* styles: with the argument `styleOptions` of `tmapSubmitOptions()`, a style such as `"cobalt"` gets options for the new mode, e.g. a dark basemap;
* basemaps: different modes have different basemaps. `tmapSubmitBasemapEquivalents()` declares which basemaps are similar across modes (e.g. light gray, dark, or satellite), so that a map can be shown in another mode with a similar basemap.

## Map components

A map component, such as `tm_geocoder()` of **tmap.mapgl**, is a `tm_element()` with the subclass `c("tm_<component>", "tm_component")`, and methods `tmap<Mode>CompPrepare()`, `tmap<Mode>CompWidth()`, `tmap<Mode>CompHeight()`, and `tmap<Mode>CompPlot()` for each mode in which it is available. Components are positioned and grouped by tmap (see [component layout](https://r-tmap.github.io/tmap/articles/adv_positions)).

## Scales

A scale determines how data values are mapped to visual values, and what the legend looks like. A new scale is rarely needed: the existing scales cover most data types, and their arguments are flexible. It is also the most difficult extension, since a scale has to handle all map variables, missing values, legends, and charts. A scale consists of two functions:

* `tm_scale_<name>()`, which returns the scale arguments as a list with class `c("tm_scale_<name>", "tm_scale", "list")` and the element `FUN`, the name of the function that applies the scale;
* that function, e.g. `tmapScaleComposition()`, which maps the data values to visual values, and creates the legend and chart.

The scale functions of tmap, such as `tmapScaleIntervals()`, are a good starting point. See `tmap.glyphs::tm_scale_composition()` for an example: a scale for the composition of a glyph, which is used together with a new layer.

## Ideas

There is plenty of room for new extensions. Some ideas: other glyph types, such as radar charts; flow maps; hexagonal binning (as a spatial transformation); new modes, e.g. based on **deck.gl** or **highcharter** (for which proofs of concept exist); and spatial data classes of other packages. Feel free to reach out via [GitHub](https://github.com/r-tmap/tmap/issues).
